metadata.file_name: 130. Kalaycı-Alas & Demir. (2023). Heuristic analysis of the native language curriculum of  successful countries in pisa and turkey by using anfis.pdf
metadata.title: HEURISTIC ANALYSIS OF THE NATIVE LANGUAGE CURRICULUM OF SUCCESSFUL COUNTRIES IN PISA AND TURKEY BY USING ANFIS

survey_design.weight_fields_interpretation: This study does not analyze student microdata from PISA; instead, it performs document analysis of native language curricula from selected countries and links curriculum content counts to published PISA 2018 reading scores. Because the dependent variable is country-level PISA performance (not student-level PV-based achievement), complex survey weights and replicate weights are not applicable in the usual ILSA sense. The paper does not report any use of sampling/survey weights or replicate-weight procedures, and it does not describe any student-level filtering or missingness handling typical of PISA microdata analyses. The main data preparation step is coding curriculum documents into counts of learning outcomes and codes for language skills, then using these counts as ANFIS inputs.

data.handling_not_reported_explanation: The analysis uses country-level PISA reading scores (2018) as the output and curriculum-derived counts (number of learning outcomes and number of codes) as inputs, rather than student-level cognitive achievement scores with Plausible Values. As a result, PV-specific procedures (e.g., Rubin’s rules across PVs) are not part of the workflow. The manuscript also does not describe any missing-data strategy for the curriculum coding process or for the country-level dataset construction, which is a reporting gap given that some countries’ program materials (e.g., Finland’s digital version) were compiled from multiple sources.

sample_details.sample_filtering_criteria: The analytic dataset is constructed at the country level by selecting nine countries (Singapore, Hong Kong, South Korea, Ireland, Finland, Canada, Sweden, the United States) plus Turkey, based on their reading performance patterns in PISA across 2012, 2015, and 2018. For each country, the authors obtain the native language curriculum documents from official education ministries and code the content into counts of (a) learning outcomes and (b) codes/themes for four language skills (listening, speaking, reading, writing), with grammar/other components treated as part of the curriculum content but the ANFIS inputs focused on the four-skill combinations. Finland’s digital program was not reached and was compiled from multiple sources before coding. The ANFIS modeling uses PISA 2018 reading scores as the output and creates four separate models corresponding to input combinations: reading+listening, reading+speaking, reading+writing, and reading+listening+speaking+writing.

main_findings.dataset_used: PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) + native language curriculum coding (2018 alignment)
main_findings.standardized_conclusion: Using PISA 2018 Reading (country-level scores) together with native language curriculum coding, the study leveraged reading and listening curriculum code counts and learning-outcome counts to predict PISA 2018 reading scores, finding that the relationship was moderately strong (R2≈0.78) with RMSE≈20.57. This indicates that aligning reading with listening-focused curriculum components may be more informative for reading performance than treating all language skills as a single undifferentiated package, though the country-level design prevents causal claims.

data.outcome_summary: The study constructs a country-level dataset by coding native language curriculum documents from Singapore, Hong Kong, South Korea, Ireland, Finland, Canada, Sweden, the United States, and Turkey into counts of learning outcomes and codes/themes for listening, speaking, reading, and writing. It then uses ANFIS (implemented in MATLAB) to model the relationship between these curriculum counts and PISA 2018 reading scores, creating four separate models for different input combinations. Model fit is strongest for reading+speaking (R2=0.851708; RMSE=13.5731) and reading+writing (R2=0.844698; RMSE=8.7802), while the integrated four-skill model is weaker (R2=0.683623; RMSE=17.3951). The paper also reports that countries with fewer learning outcomes (e.g., Singapore) can still achieve high PISA performance, implying that quality/strategic alignment may matter more than quantity. Limitations include the absence of student-level PV modeling, lack of reported missing-data handling for curriculum coding, and the correlational nature of document-to-score associations.
